Ion Exchange Chromatography: The Electrostatic Mechanism

Earlier modules emphasized volatility, partitioning, adsorption, and hydrophobic selectivity. Ion exchange works differently: analytes compete with mobile counter-ions for fixed charges on the stationary phase. Today: how that exchange equilibrium works.

Prof. Jun-Ray Macairan·Fall 2026

CHEM 3400H
Section 01

The Electrostatic Exchange Mechanism

01
CHEM 3400H

A retention mechanism built on charge, not partitioning

GC and HPLC can involve partitioning or adsorption, with retention shaped by volatility and intermolecular interactions. Ion exchange instead emphasizes electrostatic competition: ionic groups immobilized on the stationary phase attract oppositely charged analytes, displacing an equivalent amount of counter-charge. One divalent analyte, for example, can replace two monovalent counter-ions.
The distribution coefficient K from Lecture 6 still describes how strongly an analyte is retained, but here it is governed by charge and ionic competition rather than solubility or polarity matching.
CHEM 3400H

Ion-exchange sites and counter-ions

The stationary phase carries covalently immobilized ionic groups, such as sulfonate for strong cation exchange or quaternary ammonium for strong anion exchange. Weak-exchanger groups remain attached as well, but their ionization changes with pH. Each fixed charge is initially paired with a small, mobile counter-ion, typically Na⁺ or Cl⁻, that can be displaced.
Retention happens when an analyte ion in the mobile phase displaces one of these mobile counter-ions to pair with a fixed charge instead, an equilibrium that is entirely reversible.
CHEM 3400H

Competition for ion-exchange sites

For a cation exchanger, retention of analyte cation A⁺ can be written as an exchange with the resin's mobile counter-ion: R-Na + A⁺ ⇌ R-A + Na⁺. The equilibrium constant for this exchange, together with the competing counter-ion's concentration in the mobile phase, sets the analyte's distribution coefficient and therefore its retention.
Raising the concentration of the competing ion drives the equilibrium toward the mobile phase. This is the basis of salt-gradient elution.
CHEM 3400H

Which exchanger catches the analyte?

+
−
+
−
−   −   −   −

First decide the analyte's net charge at the working pH.

Opposite charges attract.
Cation and anion exchangers are named for the analytes they retain, not for the fixed charge on the resin.
For proteins, compare the working pH with pI before choosing the exchanger.
CHEM 3400H

Worked example: which ion elutes first on a cation exchanger?

A cation exchange column separates Na⁺, Ca²⁺, and Fe³⁺ under identical isocratic conditions.
Which ion elutes last, and why?
Step 1: Identify what the resin retains
A cation exchanger retains positively charged ions. Under otherwise similar conditions, stronger electrostatic attraction generally increases retention.
Step 2: Predict the order
Fe3+ will often be retained more strongly than Ca2+ or Na+, so Fe3+ is expected to elute last.
Step 3: State the limitation
Charge alone does not guarantee the order. Hydration, resin selectivity, eluent composition, and complex formation must also be considered.
CHEM 3400H
Section 02

Resin Chemistry and Capacity

02
CHEM 3400H

“Strong” describes charge persistence, not binding strength

Choose an exchanger family.

The functional group decides whether capacity changes with pH.
The words strong and weak refer to ionization of the resin group.
A strong exchanger can retain weakly if ionic strength is high or the analyte carries little charge.
CHEM 3400H

The matrix carries the charge, and its own trade-offs

Cross-linked polystyrene-divinylbenzene resins are rugged and widely used for small-ion analysis such as water testing. Silica-based exchangers offer higher efficiency for HPLC-scale separations but are limited to a narrower pH range. Agarose and other soft gel matrices are the standard for protein and biomolecule purification, where large pore size and gentle, non-denaturing conditions matter more than mechanical rigidity.
This mirrors the stationary-phase trade-offs from Lecture 10 and Lecture 14: matrix choice follows the analyte's size and the separation's purpose, not a single "best" material.
CHEM 3400H

How much can the resin actually hold?

Ion exchange capacity, typically expressed in milliequivalents per gram or per milliliter of resin, measures the total number of fixed charged sites available to exchange with analyte ions. It sets the upper bound on how much sample can be loaded before the column saturates.
This is the ion exchange analogue of column capacity discussed for GC and HPLC (Lecture 6, Lecture 14): exceed it, and peaks distort exactly as an overloaded partition column would.
CHEM 3400H

Ion-exchange capacity and breakthrough

Breakthrough capacity is the practical loading limit at which analyte begins to elute before fully binding, because all readily accessible fixed sites are occupied. It is generally lower than the total exchange capacity because not every site is equally accessible during a flow-through load.
Overloading an ion exchange column produces the same practical symptom overload always produces: early breakthrough, peak fronting, and lost resolution.
CHEM 3400H

Worked example: purifying a small protein from a crude lysate

A lab needs to purify a small, stable protein from a complex mixture using ion exchange as a first, high-capacity step.
Which matrix and exchanger type make sense?
Step 1: Choose a suitable matrix
An agarose-based medium is a common starting choice for preparative protein work because it offers biomolecule-accessible pores and aqueous, non-denaturing operation.
Step 2: Choose the exchanger type
Select cation or anion exchange from the protein’s isoelectric point relative to the working pH.
Step 3: Confirm the operating window
Silica or polymeric media may also work when their pore structure, pressure tolerance, and chemical limits fit the protein and method.
CHEM 3400H
Section 03

Selectivity, pH, and Elution Control

03
CHEM 3400H

Not all ions of the same charge are held equally

The selectivity coefficient describes how strongly the resin prefers one ion over another of the same charge, driven by ionic radius, polarizability, and degree of hydration. Generally, higher charge, smaller hydrated radius, and higher polarizability increase affinity for the fixed charge.
This is a direct analogue of the selectivity factor from Lecture 6: it explains why two ions of identical charge can still separate cleanly on the same column.
CHEM 3400H

Protein charge relative to its isoelectric point

This protein has pI 6.0. Choose the mobile phase pH and predict whether it binds a cation exchanger, an anion exchanger, or neither strongly.

Cation exchangers carry fixed negative groups and retain positively charged solutes. Anion exchangers carry fixed positive groups.
CHEM 3400H

Salt-gradient elution

Increasing the mobile phase's ionic strength, typically by raising salt concentration in a gradient, increases competition from mobile counter-ions for the fixed charges, progressively displacing bound analytes in order of increasing affinity.
A salt gradient in ion exchange plays the same functional role an organic-modifier gradient plays in reversed-phase HPLC (Lecture 13): a controlled way to sweep through a range of elution strength in a single run.
CHEM 3400H

Ion exchange and reversed phase

PropertyReversed-phase HPLCIon exchange Primary retention factorHydrophobic partitioningElectrostatic attraction Main elution controlOrganic modifier gradientSalt (ionic strength) gradient Role of pHControl ionization and selectivitySet analyte and resin charge state
CHEM 3400H

Variables that control ion-exchange retention

  • Exchanger type (cation vs anion) must match the analyte's charge sign at the working pH.
  • pH sets whether, and how strongly, the analyte and resin carry the charge that binding depends on.
  • Ionic strength is a primary control for eluting bound analyte.
  • Resin matrix and capacity set the practical scale and gentleness of the separation.

CHEM 3400H
Key Takeaways & Looking Ahead

Ion-exchange retention

  • Fixed charges on the resin exchange with mobile counter-ions; analyte ions compete for those same fixed sites.
  • Cation vs anion exchange, and strong vs weak, are chosen to match the analyte's charge behavior across the working pH range.
  • pH sets whether the analyte carries a charge at all; ionic strength is a main control for elution.
  • Exchange capacity and resin matrix set the practical loading limit and gentleness of the separation.
Next lecture: turning this theory into working methods, buffer selection, detection strategies, and real applications in water analysis and protein purification.
